facts.statement: Parry lived from 1790 to 1855, entered the Royal Navy in 1803 and served under John Ross in 1818.
In 1819 Parry led the expedition in Hecla and Griper. The ships wintered at Melville Island, and the journal appeared in 1821.
Parry kept meteorological records on Hecla. He became Hydrographer to the Admiralty in 1825 and led a polar expedition in 1827.

interpretation.statement: The contrast between sailing and wintering is a reading of the structure of the 1821 journal.

appraisal.statement: The assessment of the journal’s account of life in the ice is the publisher’s reading.

en.description: William Edward Parry’s voyage in Hecla and Griper, his winter at Melville Island, and the journal he published in 1821.
en.tagline: A winter in the ice at Melville Island
en.intro: In 1819 William Edward Parry took Hecla and Griper through Lancaster Sound in search of a passage to the Pacific. When the ice closed around Melville Island, the crews cut their way into Winter Harbour and prepared to stay.
en.orientation: The voyage changed pace when the ships stopped. Parry’s journal turns from the distance made under sail to the work of keeping a crew healthy and occupied through an Arctic winter.
en.bridge: The AETERNUS edition follows the text of 1821 and includes twenty plates and charts, a chronology and a glossary.
origin: Parry entered the Royal Navy in 1803. In 1818 he commanded Alexander on John Ross’s Arctic expedition. The Admiralty gave him command of a new expedition the following year.
career: Parry led further Arctic voyages and became Hydrographer to the Admiralty in 1825. In 1827 he set out on an expedition towards the North Pole.
literature: The journal records the search for a sea route alongside the weather, the condition of the ice and the daily life of the crews. Parry’s meteorological notes from Hecla survive in the National Maritime Museum.
en.legacy: The account of Winter Harbour shows what an expedition had to do when the next stage of the voyage was beyond its control.
